title: Grant Deed vs. Quitclaim Deed in California: What's the Difference?
content_html:
Why the Type of Deed Matters

A deed is the legal document that actually transfers ownership of real property from one person or entity to another. In California, the two deed types you'll encounter most often are the grant deed and the quitclaim deed. They can look similar on paper — both are recorded with the county and both move title — but they carry very different legal promises about what the person signing away the property actually owns and guarantees. Understanding that difference matters whether you're buying a home, taking a family member off a title after a divorce, or adding a spouse to a deed.

What a Grant Deed Is

A grant deed is the standard deed used in most California home sales. When a seller signs a grant deed, California law implies two specific promises, even though the deed itself may not spell them out in those words: first, that the seller has not already transferred the property to someone else, and second, that the property is being transferred free of any encumbrances made by the seller, except those already disclosed to the buyer. These implied warranties come from the California Civil Code provisions governing grant deeds.[1]

In practical terms, a grant deed tells the buyer: "I own this, I haven't already sold it to anyone else, and I haven't quietly put a lien or restriction on it that you don't know about." That's meaningfully more protection than simply saying "I hereby transfer whatever interest I might have."

Because of these built-in assurances, grant deeds are the norm in arm's-length purchase transactions — the kind most buyers and sellers go through when a home changes hands on the open market. Combined with a policy of title insurance, a grant deed gives a buyer a reasonably solid legal foundation for their new ownership interest.

What a Quitclaim Deed Is

A quitclaim deed makes no such promises. It simply transfers whatever interest the person signing it currently holds — if any — without warranting that the interest is valid, that it's free of liens, or even that the signer owns anything at all. If the person signing a quitclaim deed actually owns nothing, the deed transfers nothing, and the person receiving it has no legal recourse based on the deed itself.

This makes a quitclaim deed a poor tool for an arm's-length sale where the buyer is paying money and needs assurance about what they're getting. But it's a very common and appropriate tool in situations where the parties already know and trust the property's history and simply need to formally document a change in who holds title. Typical uses include:

  • Removing a spouse or ex-spouse from title after a divorce settlement
  • Adding a spouse to title after marriage
  • Transferring property into or out of a family trust
  • Clearing up a "cloud" on title, such as an old, unreleased interest from a prior owner
  • Gifting property between family members

In each of these cases, the parties generally already know what they're dealing with, so the lack of warranties in a quitclaim deed isn't a practical concern the way it would be for a stranger buying a home sight-unseen off the open market.

Side-by-Side: The Core Difference

The clearest way to think about the distinction is this: a grant deed comes with legal assurances about the seller's ownership and any undisclosed encumbrances; a quitclaim deed comes with none. Neither deed type guarantees that the property is free of all liens, unpaid taxes, or other title defects — that broader protection is what a title insurance policy is designed to cover, separate from the deed itself.

Neither deed type, by itself, transfers anything until it's properly signed, notarized, and delivered — and in California, it isn't part of the public record, and therefore isn't reliable notice to future buyers or lenders, until it's recorded with the county recorder.[2] If you're curious about what else gets recorded alongside a deed at the close of a typical transaction in this area, a related article covers what documents get recorded at closing in Riverside County.

Why a Buyer Should Care Which Deed They're Getting

If you're purchasing a home through a standard sale, you should expect to receive a grant deed, not a quitclaim deed. A quitclaim deed showing up in a purchase transaction — especially one where you're paying full market value — is a signal to slow down and ask questions. It could mean the seller isn't fully confident in their own chain of title, or it could simply reflect an inexperienced preparer using the wrong form. Either way, it's worth flagging with your agent or a real estate attorney before moving forward.

This is also where title insurance plays its most important role. Because neither deed type guarantees a defect-free title against the whole world, a title company's search of the public record — followed by an insurance policy protecting against what that search might have missed — is what actually protects a buyer's investment, regardless of which deed conveys the property.

Why a Seller Should Care Too

If you're selling property and signing a grant deed, you're making a legal statement about your ownership, even if you never say the words out loud. If it later turns out you'd already conveyed an interest to someone else, or that you'd placed an undisclosed lien on the property before the sale, a grant deed's implied warranties can expose you to liability that a quitclaim deed would not have. Sellers in family transactions — gifting a property to a child, for instance, or settling a divorce — often use a quitclaim deed deliberately, precisely because they aren't making a sale and don't want to take on warranty obligations for a property whose full history they may not be positioned to vouch for.

Other Deed Types You Might Encounter

Grant deeds and quitclaim deeds are the two you'll see most often, but California recognizes other deed forms as well, including interspousal transfer deeds (a specific-purpose variant often used between spouses for tax or title-clarity reasons) and trust transfer deeds (used to move property into a living trust). Each serves a narrow purpose, and the right one depends on the specific transaction. If you're unsure which applies to your situation, it's worth a conversation with a real estate attorney or, for sale transactions, your real estate agent, before signing anything.

A Note on Recording and Public Record

Whichever deed is used, recording it with the county is what puts the transfer on the public record and protects the new owner's interest against later claims by third parties. This is a distinct step from the deed's signing — a signed but unrecorded deed can still create real legal rights between the parties, but it doesn't give the same protection against someone else recording a competing claim first.[2] If you're in the middle of a purchase, understanding this recording step alongside the rest of the closing process can help demystify what's happening behind the scenes; our guide to what to expect during escrow walks through that timeline in more detail.

Bottom Line

A grant deed and a quitclaim deed both move title, but they are not interchangeable. A grant deed carries implied legal assurances about the seller's ownership and undisclosed encumbrances, making it the standard choice for arm's-length home sales. A quitclaim deed carries no such assurances and is best suited to transfers between parties who already trust and understand the property's history, such as family transfers or divorce settlements. Knowing which one you're dealing with — and why — is a small detail that can save a lot of confusion, or worse, down the road.

mainEntity.name: Is a quitclaim deed less secure than a grant deed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in terms of legal assurance. A grant deed includes implied promises that the seller hasn't already transferred the property and hasn't placed undisclosed encumbrances on it. A quitclaim deed makes no such promises — it only transfers whatever interest the signer actually has, if any.

mainEntity.name: Can a quitclaim deed be used to buy a home in California?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be used, but it's unusual and generally not advisable for a typical arm's-length purchase, since the buyer would receive no assurance about the seller's ownership. Grant deeds are the standard for purchase transactions.

mainEntity.name: Does either deed guarantee the property is free of liens?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Neither a grant deed nor a quitclaim deed guarantees the property is free of all liens or title defects. That protection typically comes from a title search and title insurance policy, which is separate from the deed itself.
